\section{Overview}

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Existential and Universal Length Step]
\lean{Complexity.qStep}
\statementsource{Yap83}{pdf-1a201b302069-p007-b004}
\label{Complexity.qStep}
\leanok
Let $m$ be a natural number and $Q$ a property of Boolean strings. If the Boolean
parameter is true, the step holds exactly when some Boolean string of length $m$
satisfies $Q$; if it is false, the step holds exactly when every Boolean string of
length $m$ satisfies $Q$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Alternating bounded quantifiers]
\lean{Complexity.altQuant}
\statementsource{Yap83}{
  pdf-1a201b302069-p002-b002,
  pdf-1a201b302069-p007-b004
}
\label{Complexity.altQuant}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.qStep, Turing.pairEncode}
Let $V$ be a language of bit strings, let $m$ and $k$ be nonnegative integers, let $b$
be either true or false, and let $w$ be a bit string. At depth zero, the predicate holds
exactly when $w\in V$. At each additional level, if $b$ is true it requires some bit
string $u$ of length $m$, and if $b$ is false it requires every bit string $u$ of length
$m$; in either case the predicate then holds at depth $k$ with the Boolean choice
switched and the input replaced by the self-delimiting pairing of $w$ and $u$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Zero-round alternating predicate]
\lean{Complexity.altQuant_zero}
\label{Complexity.altQuant_zero}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.altQuant}
\difficulty{1}
Let $V$ be a language of binary strings, let $m\in\mathbb{N}$, let $b$ be either the
existential or universal quantifier, and let $w$ be a binary string. The alternating
predicate at zero rounds holds for $w$ exactly when $w\in V$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Successor step for alternating quantifiers]
\lean{Complexity.altQuant_succ}
\label{Complexity.altQuant_succ}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.altQuant, Complexity.qStep, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{1}
Let $V$ be a language of binary strings, let $m,k\in\mathbb{N}$, let $b$ be either the
existential or universal quantifier, and let $w$ be a binary string. The alternating
predicate at $k+1$ rounds with initial quantifier $b$ holds for $w$ exactly when the
corresponding quantifier $b$ over strings $u$ of length $m$ holds for the predicate at
$k$ rounds with the opposite initial quantifier, evaluated on the pair encoding of $w$
and $u$.
\end{theorem}

\uses{Complexity.altQuant, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{1}
Let $V$ be a language of binary strings, and let $m,k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $w$ be a binary
string. In the alternating quantifier construction, the predicate at $k+1$ rounds with
initial universal quantification holds for $w$ exactly when, for every binary string $u$
of length $m$, the predicate at $k$ rounds with initial existential quantification holds
on the pair encoding of $w$ and $u$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Complement of an Alternating Quantifier]
\lean{Complexity.not_altQuant}
\label{Complexity.not_altQuant}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.altQuant, Complexity.altQuant_false_succ, Complexity.altQuant_true_succ}
\difficulty{4}
Let $V$ be a language of bit strings, let $m,k$ be nonnegative integers, let $b$ be a
Boolean specifying existential quantification when true and universal quantification
when false, and let $w$ be a bit string. The negation of the assertion that $w$
satisfies the $k$-level alternating quantifier condition for $V$, with each quantified
string of length $m$ and successive quantifiers alternating, is equivalent to the
corresponding condition for the complement of $V$, with the initial quantifier switched.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Alternating quantifier class]
\lean{Complexity.altClass}
\statementsource{Yap83}{pdf-1a201b302069-p007-b004}
\statementsource{BGS75}{pdf-2459e3840724-p010-b006}
\label{Complexity.altClass}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.P, Complexity.altQuant}
Let $b$ be a Boolean value and let $i$ be a nonnegative integer. A language $L$ belongs
to this class if there are nonnegative integers $C,c$ and a polynomial-time language $V$
such that, for every bit string $x$, membership $x\in L$ is equivalent to the
alternating-quantifier predicate for $V$, with initial choice $b$, depth $i$, and
quantifier-string length $C(|x|+1)^c$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Sigma levels of the polynomial hierarchy]
\lean{Complexity.SigmaP}
\statementsource{Yap83}{
  pdf-1a201b302069-p003-b003,
  pdf-1a201b302069-p007-b004
}
\statementsource{BGS75}{pdf-2459e3840724-p010-b006}
\label{Complexity.SigmaP}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.altClass}
For a nonnegative integer $i$, the class $\Sigma_i^P$ is the alternating-quantifier
class with initial existential choice and depth $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Pi levels of the polynomial hierarchy]
\lean{Complexity.PiP}
\statementsource{Yap83}{
  pdf-1a201b302069-p003-b003,
  pdf-1a201b302069-p007-b004
}
\statementsource{BGS75}{pdf-2459e3840724-p010-b006}
\label{Complexity.PiP}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.SigmaP}
For a nonnegative integer $i$, the class $\Pi_i^P$ consists of the languages whose
complements belong to $\Sigma_i^P$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Polynomial hierarchy]
\lean{Complexity.PH}
\statementsource{Yap83}{pdf-1a201b302069-p003-b003}
\statementsource{BGS75}{pdf-2459e3840724-p010-b006}
\label{Complexity.PH}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.SigmaP}
The polynomial hierarchy is the union, over all nonnegative integers $i$, of the classes
$\Sigma_{i+1}^P$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Characterization of the existential hierarchy class]
\lean{Complexity.mem_SigmaP_iff}
\label{Complexity.mem_SigmaP_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.P, Complexity.SigmaP, Complexity.altQuant}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $i$ and every language $L$ of finite binary strings,
$L\in\Sigma_i^P$ if and only if there are natural numbers $C,c$ and a language
$V\in\mathsf{P}$ such that, for every binary string $x$, membership $x\in L$ is
equivalent to the $i$-level alternating quantifier condition over witnesses of length
$C(|x|+1)^c$, starting with an existential quantifier, with the resulting encoded string
accepted by $V$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Complement duality for alternating classes]
\lean{Complexity.compl_mem_altClass_iff}
\label{Complexity.compl_mem_altClass_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.altClass, Complexity.altQuant, Complexity.compl_mem_P, Complexity.not_altQuant}
\difficulty{4}
For every Boolean quantifier type $b$, every $i\in\mathbb{N}$, and every binary language
$L$, the complement of $L$ belongs to the alternating class with quantifier type $b$ and
$i$ quantifier steps if and only if $L$ belongs to the corresponding class with the
opposite quantifier type: $L^{c}\in\mathrm{AltClass}(b,i)$ if and only if
$L\in\mathrm{AltClass}(\neg b,i)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Characterization of the polynomial hierarchy class]
\lean{Complexity.mem_PiP_iff}
\label{Complexity.mem_PiP_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.P, Complexity.PiP, Complexity.altQuant, Complexity.compl_mem_altClass_iff}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $i$ and every language $L$ of finite binary strings,
$L\in\Pi_i^P$ if and only if there are natural numbers $C,c$ and a language
$V\in\mathsf{P}$ such that, for every binary string $x$, membership $x\in L$ is
equivalent to the $i$-level alternating quantifier condition over witnesses of length
$C(|x|+1)^c$, starting with a universal quantifier, with the resulting encoded string
accepted by $V$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Complement Alternation Characterization]
\lean{Complexity.PiP_eq_altClass}
\label{Complexity.PiP_eq_altClass}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.PiP, Complexity.altClass, Complexity.mem_PiP_iff}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $i$, the class of languages whose complements belong to
$\Sigma_i^P$ equals the class of languages characterized by $i$ alternating quantifier
blocks beginning universally, with polynomially bounded witnesses and a polynomial-time
predicate.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Complement characterization of the polynomial hierarchy]
\lean{Complexity.compl_mem_PiP_iff}
\label{Complexity.compl_mem_PiP_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.PiP, Complexity.SigmaP}
\difficulty{3}
For every integer $i\ge 0$ and every binary language $L$, the complement of $L$ belongs
to the $i$th universal level of the polynomial hierarchy if and only if $L$ belongs to
the $i$th existential level: $L^{c}\in\Pi_i^P$ if and only if $L\in\Sigma_i^P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Complement characterization of existential levels]
\lean{Complexity.compl_mem_SigmaP_iff}
\label{Complexity.compl_mem_SigmaP_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.PiP, Complexity.SigmaP}
\difficulty{1}
For every integer $i\ge 0$ and every binary language $L$, the complement of $L$ belongs
to the $i$th existential level of the polynomial hierarchy if and only if $L$ belongs to
the $i$th universal level: $L^{c}\in\Sigma_i^P$ if and only if $L\in\Pi_i^P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Zero-round alternating class]
\lean{Complexity.altClass_zero}
\label{Complexity.altClass_zero}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.P, Complexity.altClass}
\difficulty{4}
The class of binary languages represented by the alternating quantifier construction
with zero rounds, for either choice of its initial quantifier, is exactly the class of
polynomial-time decidable binary languages $\mathsf{P}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The zeroth existential level]
\lean{Complexity.SigmaP_zero}
\label{Complexity.SigmaP_zero}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.P, Complexity.SigmaP, Complexity.altClass_zero}
\difficulty{1}
The class $\Sigma_0^P$ equals $\mathsf{P}$, the class of languages decidable in
polynomial time.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The Zeroth Pi Level]
\lean{Complexity.PiP_zero}
\label{Complexity.PiP_zero}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.P, Complexity.PiP, Complexity.PiP_eq_altClass, Complexity.altClass_zero}
\difficulty{1}
The zeroth level of the polynomial hierarchy, $\Pi_0^P$, is exactly the class $P$.
\end{theorem}
